Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.

than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

npm test

This isn't a codebase full of easy wins — most obvious bugs already got fixed (the audit script's `[6] Targeted scenarios` section literally documents prior fixes: 3D web games not defaulting to Phaser, offline mobile getting PowerSync, etc.). Contribution ideas are real but modest:

**1. Wire up 5 orphaned catalog entries** (`lib/catalog.ts`, `lib/questions.ts`) — `swift`, `kotlin`, `dart`, `express`, `mysql` exist in `CATALOG` (and have full `DETAILS` entries) but no candidate list in `questions.ts` ever references them, so they can never be recommended. Verified via a one-off script diffing `CATALOG` keys against all `candidate.tech` values. Best fix: mobile is the only category (unlike web/data/backend/game/cli) missing a "Primary language" layer — add one using `swift`/`kotlin`/`dart`/`ts`, and add `express`/`mysql` as legitimate alternative candidates in the backend framework/database layers. Alternative: just delete the 5 dead entries if not adding candidates.

**2. Add a reverse dead-entry check to the audit script** (`scripts/audit.mts`) — it checks "candidate ids exist in CATALOG" (forward) but nothing checks the reverse ("every CATALOG entry is reachable by some candidate"). A ~10-line addition would have caught finding #1 automatically and prevents future catalog rot.

**3. Missing engine.ts edge-case tests** (`tests/engine.test.ts`) — no test for `recommend()` throwing on an unknown category id, and no test asserting the stable tie-break ordering (index-order when two candidates score equal) documented in the `engine.ts` comment on line 41. Both are cheap, targeted `assert` additions consistent with the existing test style.

Nothing else stood out — no deprecated-tool claims, no version-number rot, no duplicate catalog keys, `Advisor.tsx`/`page.tsx` are clean React with no logic bugs found. If forced to rank, #1+#2 together make the single best PR (fix the rot, then guard against it recurring); #3 is a smaller, independent one.
